September 20, 1983
Export Development Act

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-l 10, to amend the Export Development Act, as recorded (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs; and Motions Nos. 3 and 5 (Mr. Blenkarn).

Mr. Speaker, I am happy again to participate in this debate on yet another amendment to the legislation regarding the Canadian Export Development Corporation.
1 want to say at the beginning that I and my colleagues in the NDP, generally speaking, support the thrust of the Conservative amendments to this Bill, including this one, not because we accept the simple argument, and what some of us would think is the simple-minded argument of some, that any expanded public role or state intervention is wrong per se, because it is not. Rather, we support the thrust of the amendments before us because we believe in the safeguarding and creative processes of governmental and public accountability.
To those Members of the Conservative Party who share this rationale, and I know there are many of them, I say we agree with you. But to those other Conservatives, particularly B.C. Conservatives, such as the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), the Hon. Member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. McCuish) and the Hon. Member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook) and, in fact, most B.C. Tories who are the blood brothers, bed partners and policy partners of the Conservative Government of British Columbia, the Social Credit Government of British Columbia-1 must say that 1 cannot and will not agree with their demonstrated purpose which is to centralize public authority and to destroy even the existing mechanisms of public accountability of Crown corporations and public policy.
The B.C. Social Credit Government, the B.C. Conservative Government and all the P.C. Members I have mentioned, who have on a number of occasions gone public making it clear they are all one and they essentially believe in the same things, are part and parcel of a government policy in Victoria which has disbanded the legislative committee on Crown corporations. Meanwhile, some of the federal Tories have the unmitigated gall to say in this House that they want desperately to see the same kind of committee in order to bring our federal Crown corporations under control.
They cannot have it both ways. They and their friends in British Columbia have disbanded the legislative committee on Crown corporations, thus destroying the very kind of agency which their colleagues in the federal Parliament have advocated.
Do they speak with a forked tongue, Mr. Speaker, or are they simply confused? I prefer to believe that, because they are honourable men and women, the latter is the case. But
Canada at this time of economic difficulty and challenge cannot afford such gross confusion that says "nonaccountable state intervention and irresponsible heavy borrowing by Crown corporations and Government agencies is okay as long as it is us Tories and Socreds that do it, but it is the devil's work and the road to ruin if done by anybody else." They cannot have it both ways. We can look at the record in British Columbia to see what these people do when they have the power of government. That Government, essentially a Conservative Government, has gone from $4 billion to $14 billion or $15 billion in Crown corporation and agency debt in less than eight years. There has been an increase in that Government's Crown corporation debt by over 350 per cent in less than eight years. That is what a Conservative Government has done in the Province of British Columbia. Often this is based on totally false projections of market growth and revenue potential despite some very informed warnings to the contrary. Conservative words and actions just do not jibe. They talk one line and they follow another. They are not bad guys, just confused.
Saul Alinsky once said that the secret of successful social action is to get people to do the right things for the wrong reasons. In the case of this Progressive Conservative amendment, the Official Opposition is advocating doing the right thing for the wrong reason. But because we would never question its motives in the House, we will likely support most and possibly all the amendments in order that we may do the right thing for the right reason-to provide greater parliamentary control and public accountability, and not simply because of blind dogma.
The "tinker toy" approach of the Liberals to government must be stopped. Growth for the sake of growth is just plain dumb. I fully agree with my Conservative friend who decried the number of bureaucratic academics in Government. To that I would add the excessive number of lawyers and others, whom I would call woolly-headed idealists abounding in the circles of Government and many other institutions across the country. By "idealists", I am referring to those lawyers and academics who fall into the trap of thinking that simply because a law is passed something has actually been changed. Anyone with experience in the real world knows that that just ain't so. Unless we have the will to perform a function, unless we have enforcement mechanisms, unless we have our roots down deep in the marketplace and in the realities of the world, nothing happens simply because a few words in the law have been changed. It just does not work that way.
There has been some talk and debate, going slightly beyond the amendment generally addressing some of our export and development strategies for trade. One example of export and industrial strategy has to be the joint decision of the Government opposite and the Conservative Opposition to launch the pre-build pipeline, an issue they would like to forget. That was part of an export strategy. They have fallen flat on their faces with that, as they have fallen flat on their faces with Northeast Coal in British Columbia, a combination of provincial Government and federal Government bungling. They gave the United
September 20, 1983

States exactly what it wanted. We built a pre-build pipeline at our expense to sell our gas at cheap prices to the United States. They gave up all our leverage, as Canadian Governments have often done, for future bargaining over trade and other matters. Then they squeal because the Americans keep coming back and saying, "Cut your prices, cut your prices". We keep lowering the prices because we have no leverage left. We have no guarantees. The lever which could have been used to strengthen our economic position was thrown away. Both the Liberals and the Tories were compliant partners in the whole process.
Now we see the Conservative Government of British Columbia and the federal Liberal Government, with regard to Northeast Coal, using taxpayers' money to subsidize the export of a non-renewable resource. As was the case with the pre-build pipeline, our Japanese customers are now saying that they must have a lower price, and we have no option but to give it to them because we have thrown away whatever leverage we might have had. How long do we have to listen to these Liberal and Tory bunglers? They throw away our leverage.
One does not play poker in the international marketplace with all one's cards face up. The other guys do not play the game that way. Canada has that kind of absolutely stupid reputation. That Party on the Government side and the Official Opposition on this side still have the same naive attitude they have displayed time and time again-give the store away and wonder why others take advantage of us. 1 for one and some people in business and labour with whom I have been associated, who know a little about bargaining on both sides of the table, do not believe that we can throw away all our bargaining power and then have the unmitigated gall to complain because the rest of the world does not hand something over to us on a platter. There has to be an end to this kind of jackass, stupid bargaining. We should get on with the job of developing a country which works and of which we can be proud.

Mr. Speaker, in following so shortly after the comments of the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Peterson), 1 am pleased to join the debate and to emphasize once again that the issue is not one of trade, that the problem is not trade. It is the issue of parliamentary accountability that has plagued this Parliament. More than any other, it distinguishes the Party for which I speak this afternoon from the Party which represents the Government. I will be referring this afternoon to the continued proliferation of Crown corporations and the lack of parliamentary accountability.
The Auditor General noted seven years ago that the majority of Crown corporations lacked financial management and fiscal control. Four years ago the Lambert report indicated that existing provisions for classifying Crown corporations and the accountability of each had been rendered obsolete. Just one year ago the Auditor General warned Canadians that the growing practice of using Crown corporations to conduct a widening range of Government activities has so strained our accountability framework that Parliament may not be able to
Export Development Act
exercise its fundamental responsibility for overseeing receipts and disbursements of public funds.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. We are dealing with Bill C-110, an Act to amend the Export Development Act.
Why don't you read the amendment?

It is part of the accountability process involved in this particular Act. The reason the Hon. Member is debating this Bill is that a provision is built into the Act that every now and again we have to come back before the House in order to change it.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. Obviously the Minister is making a speech.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Is it accountability or lack of accountability? Bill C-110 is now the battleground, and the amendments proposed by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) have set out the position of this Party extremely well.
That is why we are here.

1 tell the Minister opposite that the vast majority of Canadian people support our position that Parliament must ultimately control the purse strings of the nation. Quite frankly, Canadians are fed up with billion dollar deficits and lame excuses. They are tired of the stonewalling and backpedalling on the Government side. People work too hard for their money to see it squandered by Crown corporations without so much as an explanation or without coming before Parliament.
We see in Bill C-110 all the elements of one more Crown corporation slipping away from Parliament's control. The Export Development Corporation has at present $10 billion in borrowing authority and $1 billion in authorized capital. Of these limits, less than $5 billion has been used up in borrowings and less than one-half of the authorized capital has been paid in.
We on this side fought the suggestion that the limits should be doubled, and we did so for a very good reason. If the Export Development Corporation needs more borrowing authority or more capital, the EDC should come to Parliament, ask for and justify that request. The Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) disagrees. He says that it is tiresome and inefficient to come to Parliament to justify the expense, and if a Minister is responsible, then what is the problem of the Opposition? Our problem has been the experience of the past. Our problem is the Post Office, VIA Rail, de Havilland, Canadair, Eldorado Nuclear, and 1 could go on. Name any Crown corporation. Year after year the deficits mount and the questions go unanswered. Meanwhile, the public goes on paying and praying. Motions Nos. 3 and 5 as well as Motions

September 20, 1983
Export Development Act
Nos. 6 and 8, seek to keep the Export Development Corporation on a responsible track.
Bill C-l 10 proposes to increase the limits of a discretionary section of the Act from $3.5 billion to $10 billion. Under this section, the Cabinet may overrule or override a decision which the board of directors of the EDC has judged not to be in the best interests of the corporation. Not a good deal for the corporation is defined in the Act as one that "would, if entered into or issued, impose upon the Corporation a liability for a term or in an amount in excess of that which the Corporation would normally undertake." Should the corporation make the decision, the Cabinet may yet decide, good deal or not, whether it chooses to approve the transaction, and it is free to do so under these provisions of the Bill. It can overrule the board of directors which it has set up. Needless to say, if the transaction proves to be a dead loss, the taxpayers are obliged to make up that loss, or the deficit.
We believe that $3.5 billion, even with today's money, is ample. Should it not be sufficient, the Government owes it to the taxpayers of Canada to come before Parliament to ask for more. There is no indication, however, that $3.5 billion is an inadequate total at present. Less than half this amount has now been used. Why the unseemly scramble for an almost threefold increase? Does the Government have more Algerian monuments in mind, or are we to become a corporation of speculators, par exellence, a superman?
The motions before us simply wish to give the Members of this House an opportunity of review, and nothing is more fair than that. The Minister has tried to downgrade this debate, as has the Parliamentary Secretary, by attacking the Opposition for not caring about trade. Of course we care about trade. Of course we are concerned with our export business, and sometimes the deficit. However, this debate is not about trade. It could have and would have taken place over any other piece of legislation seeking to remove a Crown corporation a little further from the responsibility of Parliament.
I would be rather derelict in my duties and responsibilities to my constituents, as would any Member of this House, if I did not stand in my place and make every effort to protect their hard-earned dollars. Canadians have seen from experience what happens when Parliament's control over the pursestring is weakened. Deficits and red ink financial statements are now the order of the day. It is time that stopped. We on this side have proposed amendments to put a halt to this continuing erosion of our dollar. It now behooves the Government to demonstrate that it too has respect for the taxpayers' dollar by accepting these amendments. I urge the Government, in this last minute of my time, to do so.

Mr. Speaker, at this stage in a debate it is sometimes difficult to bring a lot of new information before the House. However, when a Government is determined to resist change and resist improvements to a Bill as much as this Government, it is sometimes necessary to emphasize the points you want to make.
The amendments we are dealing with, Nos. 3 and 5 put forward by the Conservative Party, deal with the authorization for capital borrowing of the Export Development Corporation. A couple of main issues spring to my mind when we think of the Export Development Corporation. One is, as other Members have suggested, trade. Some Government Members try to make it appear that we on this side are opposed to trade. If one examines some of the facts as to what has happened with regard to trade during the last 15 years that this Government has been in power, one finds some very interesting figures staring one in the face.
At present about 30 per cent of our Gross National Product is derived from trade. We appreciate that. Others have indicated the importance of that.
Talk about the trade surplus.

The Minister talks about the trade surplus raw materials and grain products and does not mention the surplus in manufactured goods, which is way down. In 1968, the share of world trade that Canada enjoyed at that time was 5.74 per cent. In 1981, 13 years later, it was down to 3.8 per cent, close to a 50 per cent drop in the proportion of world trade that this country enjoys. That is no credit to the present Government. It indicates its lack of concern about the trade this country should be enjoying.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association looked at this problem from a different point of view. It indicated that if we were to regain our share of world trade to the extent we had in 1970, just 11 years ago, we would create 2.7 million jobs. That is the number of jobs that would have been created during the past 15 years if the Government had had a true concern about trade and not just trade in raw materials and other products which do not produce many jobs, like the manufacturing sector does.
We might ask ourselves why we have had this poor trade performance. A few moments ago we heard from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Science and Technology (Mr. Peterson). He tried to justify the present status of trade that he believes we are enjoying. He failed to acknowledge that the significant drop from 5.7 per cent to 3.8 per cent is probably because we have suffered from a lack of productivity in this country over the last number of years under this Government. We may ask why we have suffered from a lack of productivity. It probably boils down to one most significant point, which is the fact that the present Government, although it is trying to recoup its position now, has, over the years, failed to recognize the need for spending money on research and development in science and technology.
I well remember that when I first came to the House about nine years ago, the then Minister responsible for science and technology was trying to tell Canadians that we did not need to spend money on research in science and technology, that all we needed to do was to buy the research from the United States or from some western European country. The attitude
September 20, 1983

of the Government was that money did not need to be spent on science and technology. As a result, we now see that we are spending 1.2 per cent of Canada's GNP on science and technology compared to the United States which spends 2.4 per cent of its GNP on science and technology and Japan which spends 2 per cent of its GNP on science and technology. It is not surprising, therefore, to anyone who analyses the trade situation, that one of the major reasons for our difficulty is the fact that we as a country under the present Liberal Government have not been willing to spend any significant amount of money on science and technology.
Trade is the main consideration here today. The other consideration is the issue of Crown corporations. These are the background problems which lie behind the Bill that is before the House today and the amendments we are trying to introduce to this new legislation.
When looking at the issue of Crown corporations, one interesting fact that comes to mind is that they employ some 263,000 persons. That is over a quarter of a million persons. Yet I am sure that Canadians do not realize that Government Departments themselves employ fewer people than that. There are fewer public servants employed in Government Departments than in Crown corporations now. That is how far out of hand and out of control the Crown corporations have got, and many successive Auditors General have told us so. There are now roughly 25,000 more people employed by Crown corporations than by Government Departments. That, of course, does not take into account the 84,000 people in the Armed Forces.
One cannot help but think about the waste that has been shown to us over the years by the successive Auditors General with respect to Crown corporations. My colleague who is here in the House this afternoon, the Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), told an interesting story some years ago when I was a novice in the House. It was before the 1979 election, I believe, Mr. Speaker, and at that time he said that, in his view, it only took two documents to win an election. One was a description of how our tax dollars are spent and the second was the Auditor General's report. I believe that the Hon. Member for South Shore knows what he is talking about. He has campaigned in perhaps seven or eight elections.
Ten.

Ten elections, I am sorry. He said that all he had to do was to bring to the attention of his electorate in South Shore the manner in which tax dollars are spent by Crown corporations, for example, and the waste that occurs there. A research document that was prepared prior to this debate gave 18 horrendous examples of how Canadian tax dollars were wasted by the various Crown corporations.
Another interesting aspect of today's debate is the subject of the failure by the Government to be responsible to Parliament for some of its expenditures. This has been discussed a great deal during this debate. However, when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais) spoke a few moments ago, he did not even refer to that point. We are making it one of our major points, yet the Minister did not acknowledge it as being an
Export Development Act
issue. He spoke as if the accountability of the Government was not of concern to the people. I was disappointed that he did not make some reference to that particular complaint that we have.

He told me that what bothered him most about Crown corporations was their failure to have the private sector adequately represented on their boards. I found it interesting, in light of the debate we are now having regarding EDC, to hear this gentleman who is one of the strongest supporters of the Liberal Government indicate that his principal criticism of Crown corporations was their failure to meet the increasing need for more input from the private sector.
The same issue was, of course, raised by the Economic Council of Canada. It realized as well that that problem exists, and its document entitled "Intervention and Efficiency" states on page 51:
Canada is perhaps the country with the least private-sector participation in export financing decisions.
That corroborates what my Liberal friend told me at lunch the other day, and that is, that we need to have more input from the private sector.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure it is clear in general terms to Members opposite why we on this side have reservations about the Bill before us. It is question of accountability to Parliament of a Crown agency to control a very significant chunk of public money. This Bill would give it control of a very much larger chunk of public money as well. In itself, the request for more money might make some sense, although I must say that so far I do not believe that the Government has had the courtesy to try to present any sensible case for asking for such a huge increase in the ceiling put upon EDC by statute.
I say to Government Members opposite that if there is a sensible case to be made why the Export Development Corporation needs so much increase in the ceiling, to please make it.
I know that some of my colleagues on this side are concerned that EDC is being used by the Government to become another foreign agency, particularly since the Government wants to have a CIDA representative on the board. I must say that I personally may be less alarmed about the question of EDC acting as a giver of foreign aid since I was convinced by the hearings of the Special Committee on the National Trading Corporation three years ago that concessionary financing is a virtual necessity for our export community. I mean that I do not regard concessionary financing as a form of foreign aid. It is a form of promotional financing offers, such as other countries make in their credit mixed packages and such as we must make if we are to sell abroad on many major projects.
Perhaps it does cost the country money in a way, but if properly handled it is the kind of public cost that should be repaid by public benefits such as an increased revenue base for Government.
All of which is to say that I could see certain kinds of arguments that the Government might have in mind as reasons for asking now to have the ceilings on EDC increased by so much. But the Government does not appear to want to grant us the courtesy of making these or any other kind of sensible arguments to convince us that the money limits it is proposing
for EDC are really needed for the corporation's exercise of its proper purposes.
What is of very great concern on this side of the House is that the Government appears to treat the Act we are being asked to amend as a form of spending authority. It appears to want Parliament to approve enormous increases-in fact a tripling or quadrupling-in the authorized capital and loan limits on EDC, yet without going through the formal and, I suggest, sacred process of getting formal spending authority from Parliament. What the Government appears to be proposing is that the Parliament of the people, which has grown through the centuries precisely because it has held the power of the purse strings, should step aside and allow a Crown corporation to determine, in consort with the bureaucrats of the Treasury Board and the PCO, how and when to spend a big chunk of the taxpayers' money.
This is just not acceptable. We may have the greatest respect in the world for the talents and good judgment of civil servants and Crown employees, but the fact remains that this Parliament exists, as it has always existed, to provide a check upon the Crown and its employees. The bureaucrats may have good judgment and might exercise good judgment, but when it comes to making decisions about spending public funds it is not their judgment to make. It is ours, even if we exercise judgment poorly.
It seems to me to be a fundamental principle of our parliamentary system that no funds-not even one single penny- can be properly spent without some sure and certain parliamentary authority. Merely passing a Bill that increases the statutory ceiling for EDC's capitalization does not confer any kind of spending authority at all in my view. If that is so, then the Government's apparent belief that EDC can receive new appropriations of its authorized capital merely by Order in Council and without a parliamentary appropriations Bill is wrong. If it is wrong, then we should ensure, as custodians of the public purse, that we get this matter cleared up before we make any changes in the statutory ceiling on EDC.
Let me repeat the point. In my view, no matter how good the judgment of bureaucrats may be, when it comes to spending public money, it is not up to them to decide that public money may be spent. At the very most, it is the proper job of the bureaucrats to decide how this money will be spent once we here in Parliament say that it can be spent. Once again I say that even if we exercise bad judgment about spending public money, we here in Parliament are the only body in the land that can exercise any judgment, good or bad, about spending public money. That power to grant or to withhold money from the Crown is a power belonging to the people and held by us in trust as their elected representatives. This is not merely some vague or colourful historical theory. This is the actual fact, constitutionally recognized, and we are sworn to uphold the Constitution that recognizes it. We are also pledged, by our act of faith with our electors, to maintain for them the power to grant or withhold money from the Crown.
Time and again in Parliament we on this side object to the kind of attitude displayed by the Government toward the

spending of public money. It is almost the whole of what was meant when we talked about bypassing Parliament. It may be in the nature of governments to want to exercise power without any controls. Apparently, it is in the nature of many people at any rate. But it should certainly be in our nature as Parliamentarians to want to oppose that tendency of Government.
We have grown accustomed to watching Members on the other side of the House bark like trained seals when their Cabinet bosses tell them how to vote. However, even given that whimpering, cringing response, we should expect that Government Members who are afraid to challenge their Cabinet bosses here in the House would sit down privately with them and explain the limits to them. Something very important is leaching out of our system of government if Parliament goes along with the trampling of its control over the public purse.
Therefore, my colleague for Mississauga South (Mr. Blen-karn) has proposed amendments that would deny the Government increases in the ceilings that it wants to use as a signed blank cheque. What I would like to see is an Export Development Corporation that serves the needs of Canada's exporting community in a broad sense. I suspect 1 may be less restrictive than some of my colleagues in my understanding of what kinds of functions properly fall in this mandate. And yet, equally with them, I want to see EDC preserved as an instrument that serves only our export aims, and not our unrelated foreign policy aims. It is merely a failure of imagination or administrative competence if the Government cannot manage its foreign policy aims without corrupting the functions of agencies like the EDC. At the moment, however, EDC is not short of money or of borrowing authority. If we accept the amendments of my colleague from Mississauga South, we are not going to starve the corporation. What we are going to do is to say, as a Parliament, that we are not sent here to give away power over the public purse but to retain it and to exercise it. And so I say to Members opposite, that whether they want to speak in private to their Cabinet overlords to persuade them to accept our amendments or withdraw the Bill, or whether they are willing to stand up and be counted here in the House, they should in either case accept and support the amendments proposed by my colleague.
1 think it is clear to all Members opposite that the public has not been impressed with their stewardship of the public purse and their management of the country's economic affairs. It is no good blaming mismanagement on the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Cabinet if Members opposite continue to vote with them and never act as they were sent here to act. So I say to Members opposite that we look to them to act as we do, ensuring that the parliamentary controls over EDC are not weakened but that we begin to reassert our historical authority over public spending. I urge support of the amendments proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South.

Mr. Speaker, in joining to support this amendment I should like to say that it is of basic
Export Development Act
importance that Members opposite really understand what they are doing even if they do not understand the proposals that my colleague has made with regard to Bill C-110. Somewhere along the road we do have to put a ceiling on government spending. There is absolutely no way that we can allow governments or government Crown corporations to continue to grow in the direction in which this Government has been allowing them to go now for approximately 18 years, and more especially in the last three or four years.
We are not speaking against exports. Many of my colleagues have stated that we are not debating that issue at all. We recognize that there is ample room for more export than we have ever had before because we have a $20 billion deficit and because our industries are running at only about 80 per cent capacity. Therefore, there is ample room for business to catch up in Canada and get the show back on the road.
It has not been a lack of funding that has created this situation, it has been a lack of initiative and the political climate provided by the Government in order to facilitate the exporting of what we can do best.
Unfortunately, many Canadians, and I would even suggest that perhaps a large number of bureaucrats, are not even aware of the numbers or the names of many Crown corporations in Canada. I remember when AECL was before the Public Accounts Committee. Each day Government Members would come in and give an increased number of Crown corporations. You would remember that, Mr. Speaker. It was an embarrassment to them. 1 would wager today there is not a Canadian, in the Civil Service or elsewhere, who would be able to put an exact figure on the number of Crown corporations we have. As a result, we have to exercise some kind of control over that.
I would like to bring to the attention of the House the question put on the Order Paper by the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro). The question was answered on June 29. There we have Petro-Canada, a Crown corporation. It is just a baby as far as Crown corporations are concerned. But yet there are 33 subsidiaries to Petro-Canada at the present time. It has exploded. This is what happens unless you can exercise some kind of control over a situation like that. Further, we find one individual in particular has 23 directorships on Crown corporations. It is a massive business for the bureaucrats in which to get involved. I would hope that Members opposite would recognize just exactly what they are doing.
If the system had been working, if we had an example, then I could go along with it, and I am sure my colleagues could too. But between 1977 and 1982, Canadian productivity rose by just .3 per cent, whereas in Japan it rose 27.6 per cent; in Italy it rose 22.6 per cent; in France it rose 22.3 per cent; in Germany it rose 14.7 per cent; in the United Kingdom it rose 18.2 per cent, and in the United States it rose 3.6 per cent. But here in Canada our productivity rose .3 per cent. Extending the amount of money that is provided to this Crown corporation will not resolve the problem.

September 20, 1983
Export Development Act
We recognize one of the great institutions that we have in Canada, which I believe has a lot of credibility, the Economic Council of Canada. In its recent report, on page 51, we find this:
Canada is perhaps the country with the least private-sector participation in export financing decisions. The governments of most other industrial nations encourage bank participation in this area, more so than does the government of Canada. In six of the industrialized countries examined, the supply of primary financing is left completely in the hands of the private sector, which may, however resort to public rediscounting facilities. In most of the 17 countries studied, the negotiations for granting export credit are also left to the private sector. This is not the case in Canada, where direct negotiations take place between the EDC and the foreign buyer. When the banks are invited to participate jointly with the EDC in long-term financing, they often complain of being denied access to all the information and to the negotiations, and of being presented with ready-made proposals.
This is exactly what I was saying earlier when I said 1 do not think that any of the bureaucrats really have all the basic knowledge and information required in these situations.
The Economic Council report devoted a full chapter to the subject of export finance and the EDC. The Government Members on the other side of the House would do well to read the report before performing on cue before the proposed amendments are put to a vote. The thrust of the report is to scale down and reorientate the EDC, not to augment it. Seven of the report's 31 recommendations pertain to the EDC.
The Economic Council found that few credit and insurance gaps exist in Canada. It questioned whether or not the EDC needs to be involved in insurance and in financing when the private sector is able to meet the need. It observed that Canadian exports are not as heavily subsidized as exports in other countries, and what subsidies do exist find their way to a very limited number of firms. It recommends that the EDC do less direct financing and that the private sector do more.
These are the recommendations made by the Economic Council. I hope Members opposite will pay attention to them:
We recommend that the Export Development Corporation gradually move towards providing export credit re-insurance, leaving the field of insurance proper to the private sector. We further recommend that the Export Development Corporation serve as the insurer of last resort to close any gaps left by the private sector in the supply of export credit insurance.
We recommend that the Export Development Corporation continue to provide direct financing for Canadian sales abroad when there is reason to believe that the private sector is unable to provide the required credits. Public financing should be made available only under terms and conditions commensurate with the risks involved and the costs of such assistance-including the opportunity cost of the funds used-except in those cases where it is deemed necessary to take into consideration the export-support programs of other countries.
We further recommend that the Export Development Corporation's gradual withdrawal from most direct lending activities be accompanied by an increased concentration of its efforts in the field of credit insurance and bank guarantees. The Corporation should also stand ready to provide refinancing facilities for private lending institutions engaged in export finance.
We recommend that the federal Government continue its efforts, at meetings of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development and the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, to obtain an international agreement to further limit subsidized export credit. In the absence of such an agreement, we recommend that Canada use subsidized credit only in cases where there is a sufficiently strong presumption that it will facilitate the opening of new markets, or that it will increase the market share for Canadian products.
We recommend that, in the absence of an international agreement to further limit subsidized export credit, the federal Government consider the advisability of matching foreign export-support programs that currently have no equivalent in Canada and of providing assistance to domestic firms which must compete with imports that have benefited from foreign subsidized credits.
We recommend that the private sector be encouraged to supply direct export credits to Canadian producers even when a public subsidy is deemed necessary. The federal Government, through the Export Development Corporation, should assume the cost difference between the preferential conditions offered and the conditions that would have prevailed had private financing been offered in the absence of public support.
We recommend that the Export Development Corporation manage separately those of its activities that are intended to expand markets for Canadian products. We further recommend that provision be made for greater co-ordination between the Export Development Corporation and the Canadian International Development Agency whenever their activities overlap.
I apologize for reading these recommendations. I know it is always boring, but I wanted to bring to the attention of Hon. Members opposite what the Economic Council of Canada indicated. I thank the House for the opportunity to present it at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I support Motions Nos. 6 and 8 in the name of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), and I want to give the reasons for saying so. Government Members might be somewhat surprised by the manner in which the Official Opposition is speaking out on this Bill. They might have felt there would be a period of time in the House when Opposition Members would make their case and then silently slip away into the night. I am sure that was the Minister's hope. The reason the Official Opposition is so adamant and that many of its Members are speaking on these various motions is that the Bill has finally given us a vehicle with which to press home the point that Canadians are not satisfied with the financial accountability the Government has applied to the use of taxpayers' money.
Whether one speaks about the Export Development Corporation, other Crown corporations or the daily administration of Government itself, Canadians across the country are concerned about the lack of accountability. Unless Government Members are willing to make some changes and to come to some understanding on the motions that have been moved, they might have to sit for some period of time yet to hear the case we are making on behalf of Canadians. We intend to keep making the case.
Motion No. 6, which was adequately described by the mover, would allow the Government of Canada to increase the limit on promissory notes to $10 billion from the present $3.5 billion. When one looks at that motion, it is interesting to note that the Government has come to the House of Commons with a request to increase the limit to $10 billion when in fact it has not expended the present limit. 1 understand it has expended about $460 million, leaving over $3 billion or roughly 80 per cent of the present limit. Surely the first question which must be asked is why the Government wants to increase the limit if the present limit has not been expended in the first place.
The Government cannot simply be given a blank cheque, because our past experience with its profligate spending and its
September 20, 1983

desire to operate outside Parliament or away from the scrutiny of Parliament would allow it to do so again in spades, even more than what is presently in place. The Government has not been able to expend the limit, yet it wants the limit increased. The Minister and his supporters do not give us the reasons for this.
1 ask Government Members whether or not they have asked their Minister why he wants it increased from $3.5 billion to $10 billion. If they have asked him, which 1 doubt, even more important, are they able to explain to the Canadian public why the Export Development Corporation, through the Government, needs a $10 billion limit rather than the $3.5 billion which is not being totally used at present? I am sure they have not asked the Minister about this.
It is not only the Opposition which should hold the Government accountable. Government Members should hold their own Ministers accountable, and I suggest they are not doing it.
I do not know why the Government would want to come to Parliament and request an increase in the limit when at present it is only expending 20 per cent of the $3.5 billion. This is what we are being asked to do.
Motion No. 8 would allow loans through the Consolidated Revenue Fund to be increased from the present limit of $2.5 billion to $10 billion. Again we find that the Government has not reached the present limit in this respect. It is at some $700 million as against the $2.5 billion limit. I will not make the argument again about why it asks for more when even this profligate Government has not expended it to the limit. What is more important is that we would allow these expenditures from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. If the Canadian public does not understand what is the Consolidated Revenue Fund, let me indicate that it is a fund that has been financed by Canadian taxpayers. It is a pot of their money. The Government is saying that it wants that limit without a vote in the House by elected Members of Parliament. This is what the Government is after.
1 ask Government Members whether they have asked the Minister how they are to explain back home an expenditure of up to $10 billion without any parliamentary vote, without any parliamentary discussion, without any parliamentary scrutiny. Have they asked, or do Government Members simply relish their reputation for asking nothing, seeing nothing, hearing nothing-
But spending everything.

They want to be allowed to sit on the right side of the Speaker; then life is complete for a Liberal. It is a little more complicated than that.
Yesterday I had an opportunity to have a discussion with a number of representatives from the private sector, people from the United States, Australia and Canada. The purpose was to have an exchange between people in the private sector and people in the public sector in terms of accountability, how Parliament functions and how it should function. Executives of
Export Development Act
the private sector simply cannot understand how Members of the Crown and executives of Crown corporations are not literally put on the griddle by their supporters on a constant basis, asking reasons why something was done in such and such a way and what is the bottom line. They cannot understand it, and neither can Canadians.
A recent poll indicated that for many Canadians Parliament is irrelevant. There are reasons for that. I will not go through all the reasons. However, I suggest that Parliament only became relevant in Britain when it was able to hold accountable those who were in charge. The reason Parliament is not important to Canadians today is that they see that that function has been largely lost by Parliament. Nobody is more to blame than the Government opposite.
There are all kinds of emoluments or certain perks that Members of Parliament may have, but do not question the real issues, such as how the Government is spending the taxpayers' money. That is the real issue. The Minister, fine chap that he might be, knows that all he has to do is to ride out the storm and eventually it will be a $10 billion limit here, a $10 billion limit there, a $60 billion limit on EDC. What can he do then? He can go and have his party with the boys at EDC. He will say, "Boys, it was a long, hard battle, but here's your money. I got it for you."
1 am being very blunt with the Minister. I say to him that it is high time that this Government came to grips with that accountability question. I see you rising, Mr. Speaker, I am sure in anticipation of my next sentences. I simply say that if the Government wants Parliament to become relevant, then let it become accountable and be willing to come under the scrutiny of accountability which I believe the Members of this House are willing to give it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise for the third time on Bill C-l 10, this time on amendments Nos. 6 and 8 proposed by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). 1 do so following the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp). I say to that Hon. Member that I wish I had thought of many of the words he contributed and to congratulate him on his speech. 1 would like to follow on what he has said because the Minister is present.
I should say to the Minister that if he would see his duty in terms of parliamentary control over spending the way he sees his obligation as a Minister to be here when his Bills are before the House, which is unusual for Members of the Liberal Cabinet, we would not have a problem. What is frustrating about this issue, and we have debated several of these issues, is that we appear to be butting our heads against the brick wall on an issue that ought to be fundamental to any Member of any government in Canada.
The Hon. Member for Provencher put the figures on the record. Let me just repeat them briefly. The funds already available under the section which amendment No. 6 deals with are $3.5 billion, of which just over $460 million have been taken up, the funds available under amendment No. 8 are $2.5

September 20, 1983
Export Development Act
billion, of which $1.4 billion have been committed but only $711 million have been advanced.
Just as important is the fact that there is unused authorization, which makes a mockery of the suggestion that more authorization is needed. Just as important, if in other sections of the Bill we were talking about the EDC in terms of its own transactions needing greater authorization, we are in this case talking about transactions which the EDC cannot finance. In both cases we are talking about either insurance guarantees or loan guarantees which require the approval of Cabinet over what for the sake of reference may be called the Cabinet's own account. Let us be clear about what that means.
The Cabinet has proposed that we consider increasing authorizations beyond what appears to be necessary in accounts the very nature of which is that the decisions to spend those moneys will not be taken by an independent or semiautonomous Crown corporation, but will be taken directly by the Cabinet, because they are not good for proper business transactions in the sense that they are too great or beyond the scope or outside what the EDC believes it can do.
We have a marriage of two principles here. We are being asked to consider increasing authorizations well beyond needed funds, based on the existing experience, to be spent in secret by the Cabinet. All Parliament will ever know is after the fact. It ought to be a simple matter to get it clear to a Minister of the Crown that everybody in this House wants to see Canadian trade expanded. This debate will go on forever about the trade aid question. There will be times when it will be necessary to use forms of EDC financing, forms of EDC guarantees, forms of CIDA aid assistance to make deals. Everybody in the business knows that. Everybody in the world is competing on those terms.
When the Cabinet has a proposal that would be good for Canadians business in its view, one that would require funds to be advanced under these sections, those sections which the Cabinet has authority over and which it believes would be good for Canadian industry and trade and job development, the principle espoused in the Bill is "We will do it, but we do not dare trust telling Parliament in advance about making those extensions of Canadian liabilities the qualities of the deal. Later we will tell you what we used your money for." The principle that ought to be near and dear to the heart of the Minister is that Parliament authorizes the spending of the money and therefore Parliament ought to consider deals that are beyond the business scope of EDC. If we cannot deal with the scope of the internal matters that relate to EDC, surely to goodness when those deals involve direct Cabinet approval because they are beyond the scope of EDC, those are exactly the situations which ought to be before Parliament for its scrutiny.
It is really that simple. Perhaps nowhere else in this Bill is this principle more important than in the sections governed by these amendments. The principle is this. If the Minister believes that selling something Canadian to another country is in the best interest of that industry and of Canada and he proposes to guarantee it, if he wishes to avoid creating the
impression that there is something to hide in that deal and avoid creating the impression that the Government proposes to create more fiascos of the nature we have seen in the last little while after the fact, then let him say one of two things now. Let him say that the Members of the Opposition are right, that Parliament should see deals that exceed the EDC natural disposition before they are made so that the Minister can get the best wishes of Parliament. Second, the Minister could say to the House that the EDC needs authorization 7, 8 or 9 times what already has been spent, or that those changes are not necessary in any sense of normal business practice.
I note the clock, Mr. Speaker, so through you, I would say that the Minister must come to recognize that the opposition on these points of fundamental principle will not go away. Parliamentary control over spending is far too important.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 45 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-PROVISION OF ALTERNATIVE SERVICE TO COMMUNITIES AFFECTED BY VIA RAIL CUTBACKS. (B) COMMUNITIES WITHOUT SERVICE
TRANSPORT-PROVISION OF ALTERNATIVE SERVICE TO COMMUNITIES AFFECTED BY VIA RAIL CUTBACKS. (B) COMMUNITIES WITHOUT SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 15, 1981, after the infamous announcement made by the then Minister of Transport indicating that it was his intention to axe 20 per cent of the nation's rail services, which threat he in fact carried out, I asked the Minister what he would do to provide alternate services to such communities as Minto and Chipman, Napodogan and Juniper, Plaster Rock and McGiv-ney and others. He informed me that bus service would be provided to those communities that were left without alternate sources of transportation. That was on December 15, 1981, Mr. Speaker.
Yesterday we were treated to an announcement by the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) that in effect there may have been some mistakes made by the former officials of VIA Rail which were, of course, sanctioned by the then Minister of Transport, and that he would ask VIA Rail to take a look at the cuts that were made with a possible view to restoring two of those lines, one of which was the Edmundston-Moncton run which would service a great many of those communities I just mentioned.
I was pleased to hear that the Minister is making that recommendation to VIA Rail officials, and I would anticipate that not only will he ask that they review it, but will suggest in strong terms that they positively favour the re-establishment of
September 20, 1983______________________ COMMONS DEBATES
that particular run between Edmundston and Moncton. 1 shall listen with a great deal of interest to the Acting Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport. No doubt he will address himself to that particular question as it is indeed of particular relevance to the question I posed to the Minister back in 1981.
I would also like to hear the Acting Parliamentary Secretary address himself to the other major cut that was made to the railways in New Brunswick, primarily the elimination of the VIA Rail service, the Atlantic Limited, which was certainly one of the most popular trains in the nation at the time and which carried approximately 240,000 passengers annually, the elimination of which left southern New Brunswick and area virtually without connection to Upper Canada and to points west.
I would like to read from an article that appeared in The Telegraph-Journal on October 7, 1981, and I quote:
Modern new trains will be coming to the Maritimes in the summer of 1983, Federal Transport Minister Jean-Luc Pepin said here Tuesday-
He said:
"That's why I'm willing to gamble. Popularity is a very, very difficult thing in life, so I'm willing to take two years of flak because people in the Maritimes and in the West, in two or three years from now, will ride in their LRCs and they'll say this guy Pepin wasn't so crazy after all, was he?"
According to The Telegraph-Journal, Mr. Speaker, he went on to say that:
-he is anxious to hear the reaction of people in Moncton and Saint John a few years from now when the light, rapid, comfortable (LRC) trains are introduced. He said he would like to hear them say "Mr. Pepin was not so nuts after all."
The summer of 1983 has come and gone and so have the hopes and aspirations of all of those in Saint John and Moncton and other areas which might have taken the word of the Minister and hoped that they would be riding on LRC trains. But in fact this did not materialize, just as the Minister of Transport of the day has dematerialized.
The comment to the now Minister would be that I would hope he will actively, even if it is in a political way, pursue the possibility, in a very positive manner, of re-establishing the Edmundston-Moncton route, as we have been pressing for, and also pursue the re-implementation of that most popular train, the Atlantic Limited, which created such a beneficial service to the residents of southern New Brunswick as it carried passengers from Moncton through Sain John to Montreal. Those people have been left without direct transportation to Montreal. They now have to travel hundreds of miles backwards to get to Montreal if they are going to take the most economical form of transportation. Who can afford air fares now, except those of us who are subsidized by the citizens of Canada so that we can travel back and forth on Air Canada?
I would leave the House with this thought. The decision that these services be eliminated must rest with the CTC. Just get those trains on and when we form the government we will ensure that they stay on.
Adjournment Debate

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: TRANSPORT-PROVISION OF ALTERNATIVE SERVICE TO COMMUNITIES AFFECTED BY VIA RAIL CUTBACKS. (B) COMMUNITIES WITHOUT SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 thank the Hon. Member for his concern about this vital matter. Undoubtedly he is expressing the concerns of many constituents who have spoken to him about the cuts in rail services to their communities. However, I believe in all honesty he would admit that he is glossing over the problems which led to the decision VIA Rail had to make several years ago to cut some of its services. It was facing an increasingly large operating deficit which was in the neighbourhood of half a billion dollars a year. The Government had to make a decision to either continue to pour money into the operating losses or cut some of the services, take some of that money and put it into spending for new capital equipment which would enable VIA Rail at some future date to have new capital equipment with which to better serve the Canadian people and attract the kind of passenger traffic which is necessary to make it a viable service.
I am sure we have all heard of the huge amounts of money it costs to transport each passenger. I am not the parliamentary secretary for this Ministry, but I believe that every time a passenger pays $1 for rail transportation the Government contributes $4 or $5 in addition.
The present Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) has directed that efforts be focused on achieving four main objectives: an improved national system of rail passenger services coast to coast; improved service to regional areas; increased operational efficiency and improved financial performance; and encouragement of feedback from the public generally and from other affected parties on Canadian rail passenger services. He is holding a meeting in Edmonton on September 29 with his provincial counterparts to discuss these matters and, hopefully, he will come up to the kind of judicious solution we expect from him. Thank you.

subtopic: ENERGY-INCENTIVES FOR OIL SANDS PROJECTS. (B) GOVERNMENT OFFER
ENERGY-INCENTIVES FOR OIL SANDS PROJECTS. (B) GOVERNMENT OFFER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 2, just prior to the summer recess at the House of Commons, I asked a question of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien). I suggested that the development of the oilsands creates thousands of jobs in virtually every sector of the Canadian economy, and particularly in Central Canada. I wanted to know whether the offer being made to BP and PetroCan on the Wolf Lake project in northeastern Alberta was being made to other oil companies to develop the vast resource of the oil sands industry in northeastern Alberta. His reply was that they could make an application and it would be reviewed by the Minister. He went on to say, and this is something to which I take serious objection:
Of course one of the problems is that many of the projects in the past were based on an ever-increasing international price for oil. We see now that the price has gone down so the economics of these projects are not the same as they were two years ago.

September 20, 1983
Adjournment Debate
Most of the difficulties are not because of the tax propositions we have put forward.
Today in Calgary the Minister of Energy and his Alberta counterpart announced that the $300 million Cold Lake project will go ahead. The reason the project is going ahead, Mr. Speaker, and 1 am reading from the press release, is that the federal Government will provide earned depletion allowance and waiver of payment of the petroleum gas revenue tax until the company has recovered its capital costs in accordance with federal budget provisions announced in April, 1983.
The Minister has the audacity to stand in this Elouse, Sir, and say to me that the economics of this project are no longer feasible, and then in a press release today, to get maximum political impact in Alberta, particularly in northern Alberta, he says that they have waived the PGRT, a tax which damn near killed the industry in western Canada and the western basin.
When I asked this question I suggested that there were thousands and thousands of jobs available if the Minister would get off his posterior and get those oil sands developed in northeastern Alberta. He states in the press release that 700 direct jobs will be created and filled primarily by residents of the Cold Lake region. Another 90 permanent jobs will result from the operational phase of the project.
My point is, Mr. Speaker, that if the Government with its national energy policy had offered this deal to Imperial Oil in the very first place we would have a $12 billion construction program in northeastern Alberta developing one plant in Cold Lake, and another $12 billion plant north of Fort McMurray developing the oil sands in that area. Rather than 90 permanent jobs each plant would create 2,000 permanent jobs. Rather than a construction force of 700, we would have a construction force of ten times that size. When we get up and ask the Minister of Energy questions concerning the effect of the PGRT on the industry in northeastern Alberta we continuously get these shuffling evasive answers and that is just not good enough. In fact, Mr. Speaker. I will not use another term which is unparliamentary but it is certainly evasive. I would think that you can imagine what I would like to say.
At two o'clock today Edmonton time, Mr. Speaker, the Minister announced with great fanfare a project to develop the oil sands in northeastern Alberta which will probably have one tenth of the impact it could have had on the constructions force. All this at a time when people are looking for jobs and cannot find them, when people are begging for jobs. Unemployment is extremely high across the country and a megaproject the size of which I am talking about multiplies the number of jobs right across the land, so there would even be increased employment in central Canada. This affects virtually every Province in the country, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: TRADE MARKS AND PATENTS-PROPOSED CHANGES IN DRUG MANUFACTURING LICENCES. (B) FORMER MINISTER EMPLOYED BY DEPARTMENT
TRADE MARKS AND PATENTS-PROPOSED CHANGES IN DRUG MANUFACTURING LICENCES. (B) FORMER MINISTER EMPLOYED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday during Question Period I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) a question concerning the Government's proposed plans to remove Section 41(4) of the Patent Act. The effect of this change in the legislation would be to substantially increase the prices of pharmaceutical drugs to Canadian consumers as well as to increase taxes generally as a result of the dramatic rise in the total cost of preventional pharmacare plans. I could perhaps provide a bit of history concerning this situation.
In 1969, the Hon. Ron Basford brought forward proposed amendments to the Patent Act which implemented a scheme of compulsory licensing. This was as a result of a report by a parliamentary committee which very clearly documented that pharmaceutical drug prices in Canada were the highest in the world at that time. It was in response to this very, very serious situation that the Government moved in 1969. As I indicated, Ron Basford brought forward legislation to in fact permit the manufacture in Canada of generic drugs. At the time, the Conservative Party bitterly opposed this change. Today, it remains silent on the proposals of the Government. In 1969, the Government moved forward despite a very serious and powerful lobby by the multinational drug corporations.
Since the legislation was enacted in 1969, I would note that drug prices in Canada have dropped quite dramatically. The availability of generic drugs, both to hospitals and to consumers, has resulted in drug prices in Canada which are significantly lower than those in the United States, for example.
Just to give a few illustrations of the impact of this important legislation, I would note that 250 milligram tablets of chlorpropamide are sold in a one thousand tablet lot in Canada for $14.07, while it cost some $281.38 in the United States.
September 20, 1983

This drug is commonly used by diabetics. As well, concerning medication for heart patients, 1,000 tablets of chlorthalidone costs $30.47 in Canada and $289.98 in the United States. This is the cost from the wholesaler to the pharmacist. As a final example, one of the most commonly used pharmaceutical drugs in Canada is diazepam, the generic name for the drug better known as Valium. Again concerning the price to the pharmacist from the wholesaler, five milligram tablets of Valium cost $3.13 per 1,000 tablets in Canada and $189.97 in the United States. Clearly the effect of the legislation introduced in 1969 was to dramatically lower the costs of a wide range of pharmaceutical drugs to Canadian consumers and provincial Governments.
Earlier this year the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs proposed to repeal this important provision. It is interesting to note that the original author of the legislation, Ron Basford, has come out strongly opposed to the proposal and in fact has indicated that the Government is caving in to the multinational drug companies.
I note as well that a number of Members even in the Government caucus are speaking out in opposition to this regressive proposal because they recognize the very significant impact it would have on Canadian consumers. I would also ask how the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) could possibly defend such a proposal. She claims on the one hand to be trying to protect Medicare, but, of course, if the proposal of her colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola), is enacted, then the cost to provincial pharmcare plans for pharmaceutical drugs will go up very significantly. Indeed, so significantly that it could seriously threaten the survival of provincial pharmacare plans. There also would be a serious job loss in the generic drug industry in Canada which currently employs some 1,300 individuals.
In my view the impact of this legislation on the sick, poor and particularly elderly Canadians, whose reliance upon pharmaceutical drugs is greater than most of the others, would be devastating. I repeat that the Government's proposal amounts to nothing less than an attack on the poor, the elderly and the sick. It is for that reason that that the federal New Democratic Party is strongly opposed to any amendments whatsoever to Section 41(4) of the Patent Act.
I noted as well in my question yesterday that the Government has refused to consult until this point with those who are most affected; the Consumers Association of Canada, the National Anti-Poverty Organization and provincial governments. All are strongly opposed to this legislation. Indeed, the only group which has been consulted is the multinational drug industry and its former lobbyist, Martin O'Connell, who is now being paid by the taxpayers of Canada to advise the Government on these proposed legislative changes.
I urge the Government to withdraw any suggestion of these amendments and not to in any way dilute compulsory licensing

in Canada. I would hope that the Government would recognize that the impact of this legislation would be very devastating, indeed, to many thousands of Canadian consumers, particularly the elderly, the poor and the sick.

subtopic: TRADE MARKS AND PATENTS-PROPOSED CHANGES IN DRUG MANUFACTURING LICENCES. (B) FORMER MINISTER EMPLOYED BY DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have often wondered how the Hon. Member could stand in the House with a straight face and make some of the outrageous exaggerations and assertions that he makes, particularly when he is trying to play with the sensibilities of the elderly, the poor and the sick, trying to score cheap political points at the expense of some of the people in our society who are least able to defend themselves.
I also argue that he is guilty of monumental hypocrisy. He and his Party are always crying about jobs. Now he is upset that the Government is showing concern about jobs in an extremely vital industry, an industry which holds so much portent for the future.

The Hon. Member ought to know, Mr. Speaker, that the current study was initiated following the shutdown of a number of drug companies, especially in the Montreal area, and that the Government of Quebec and several other provincial governments expressed serious concern about the future of that industry.

The Government's objective is to maintain low prices for consumers. I repeat that its objective it is to maintain low prices for consumers and to create a business climate that will support development of the industry with an emphasis on the growth of return, the development of exports and an active ingredient manufacturing in Canada.
The consultations are broad. Provincial Governments are being consulted. Last week, the Minister met with provincial Ministers, consumer organizations, patent holding manufacturers, generic companies and health care professionals. Also, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has expressed her concern that costs be kept low. A balance is being sought by the Government, even though that is an extremely difficult thing for the Member and his Party to understand.
With regard to Mr. O'Connell, he fully disclosed his previous association and severed all ties prior to being retained by the Minister. The Minister felt that his awareness of the company's concerns and his knowledge of government workings would be an asset in this particular review. There is no question but he is exercising his present attitudes in a fully impartial manner. I would ask the Hon. Member to stop dragging another person's name in the mud.
